newsitem.title: USA: Who will win U.S. secretary of state sweepstakes?. [CORRECTED 13:39 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Who will win U.S. secretary of state sweepstakes?. [CORRECTED 13:39 GMT]

text.p: The U.S. secretary of state sweepstakes is on.

With President Bill Clinton far ahead of his Republican rival in polls, there is increasing focus on who might succeed Warren Christopher if Clinton on Nov 5 becomes the first Democratic president re-elected since Franklin Delano Roosevelt.
Officially, this is not an issue. "We're too focused on the election to even think about what's going to happen in January," said White House spokesman Maryellen Glynn.
But speculation is heating up.
Who will be secretary of state into the 21st century is one key appointment facing Clinton, if he remains in office.
The conventional wisdom has been for some time that Christopher would leave at the end of one four-year term.

He is 71, has endured a punishing overseas travel schedule, has trouble sleeping in the best of times and his goal of an Israel-Syria peace deal is more elusive than ever. Some aides seem to take it for granted they will be looking for new jobs.
Still, he could stay on. His future will be decided only when he and Clinton sit down to talk about it, insiders say.
"The president relies greatly on Secretary Christopher. ... The president thinks he's done a terrific job," Glynn said.

Even so, presidents often make a special effort in their last term to leave a legacy. Christopher may have been suitable in the first term but even many Democratic partisans say new blood is required.

The United States faces momentous decisions like devising post-Cold War security in Europe, managing ties with Russia and China, keeping Bosnia and Mideast peace efforts alive and persuading Congress to stop slashing the diplomacy budget.

Christopher has worked tirelessly, especially on Mideast peace, but has subcontracted many key areas, like Russia, to others. He had a relatively low profile in the crisis with Iraq after failing 10 days ago to get France to join Britain and the United States in patrolling an expanded no-fly zone.
The next secretary must bring more energy and activism to the job and be able to define a broad strategic vision for U.S. policy, some experts say.

"You need to get somebody who can try to map out a post-Cold War American policy. We have not done this so far," said Michael Mandelbaum of Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies.
Some would-be successors appear to be almost campaigning for the job.

Richard Holbrooke, former assistant secretary of state who brokered the Bosnia peace deal then retired, came back into the process in July as an unpaid consultant, led a U.S. delegation to observe Bosnia elections this weekend and was named an adviser on Baltic security by Sweden.
Brilliant, creative and energetic, he understands U.S. power and how to wield it but also can be arrogant, a self-promoter and rubs many people the wrong way.

U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright took her first official trip to Turkey and endeared herself to the Cuban-American community with her condemnation of Fidel Castro and his shooting down of planes carrying Cuban-American activists.

Loyal, passionate, and anti-communist, she is an effective communicator of U.S. policy and has dealt with a panoply of issues at the U.N. If appointed, she would be the first female secretary of state. But critics wonder if she could manage the State department bureacracy and negotiate effectively.

Sam Nunn, who is retiring from the Senate, is well-regarded in Congress and a leading thinker on key issues, like Russia, China, NATO and nuclear arms. When Christopher talked of resigning in 1994, Clinton sounded out Nunn and Colin Powell, ex-chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, for the job.

But Nunn, who said on Saturday he would like the job at some point in his career and would consider an offer if Clinton is re-elected, opposes a key Clinton intiative, NATO expansion, and could challenge him on others.

Mickey Kantor, U.S. commerce secretary, is very close to Clinton and was instrumental in his 1992 election. He is regarded in the administration as excelling as U.S. trade representative, possessing energy and good management skills. But did he push the Japanese and trade too hard?

Powell, a hero of the Gulf War, remains a favourite of Clinton but some feel his chances of being secretary in a Democratic administration were diminished when he spoke on behalf of Bob Dole at the Republican convention.

Former Senator George Mitchell, Republican Senator Richard Lugar, Deputy Undersecretary of State Strobe Talbott, (Corrects by adding dropped name) National Security Adviser Anthony Lake and Ambassador to Russia Thomas Pickering are also on some lists.
